rows.name: context-16-frozen-16
rows.question: Why?
rows.answer: Because a timeout does not mean the charge failed—it may have succeeded while the response was lost. Reusing the same key lets the server recognize the retry and return the saved result, while atomic key claiming prevents concurrent requests from charging twice. The charge and its durable outcome record must commit atomically; otherwise, a crash between them leaves a charge with no record. For an external payment provider, a local transaction alone cannot guarantee this: the provider must support idempotency, or you need reliable reconciliation before retrying.

review.note: Timeoutdoesnotprovechargefailed, savedstablekey/atomicclaim and localcharge-outcomecommit close duplicate/crashgaps. Externalprovideridempotency/reliable-reconciliation separatelyqualified; no localtransactionguarantee invented.
review.usefulPrefix: Because a timeout does not mean the charge failed—it may have succeeded while the response was lost. Reusing the same key lets the server recognize the retry and return the saved result, while atomic key claiming prevents concurrent requests from charging twice.

rows.name: context-21-frozen-21
rows.question: Why?
rows.answer: Because compare-and-swap applies an update only if the current value matches your expectation. If you expected 5 but it now contains 7, retrying with 5 keeps failing while it remains 7; expecting 7 but still proposing 6 would overwrite newer progress. For an increment, use the observed 7 and recompute the desired value as 8, repeating if another change intervenes. A weak compare-and-swap can also fail spuriously, in which case the observed value may be unchanged.

rows.name: context-30-frozen-30
rows.question: Why?
rows.answer: Atomicity guarantees all-or-nothing changes, not that concurrent transactions behave as if run one at a time. Initially, Alice and Bob are both on call: each transaction reads that snapshot, checks that the other remains on call, then updates only its own row to go off call. Under snapshot isolation, those writes affect different rows, so both can commit, leaving nobody on call. No serial execution permits that result: the second transaction would see only one person remaining and fail its check.
